o: It forms within the substance of psoas major

The lumbar plexus forms within the substance of psoas major. Most branches emerge laterally; the genitofemoral emerges anteriorly, and the obturator nerve and lumbosacral trunk medially.
Psoas haematoma or abscess can affect the plexus.
The femoral nerve is formed from the posterior divisions of L2, L3 and L4

The femoral nerve is formed from the posterior divisions of L2, L3 and L4; the obturator nerve from the anterior divisions.
Posterior divisions supply extensors.
The accessory obturator nerve, when present, supplies pectineus

Last's says the accessory obturator nerve, present in about a third, comes from the posterior divisions of L3 and L4 and supplies pectineus; it would better be called an accessory femoral nerve.
It crosses the pubis.
The genitofemoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of psoas

The genitofemoral nerve emerges from the anterior surface of psoas and runs down on it, deep to the psoas fascia.
It is the only branch on the front of the muscle.
Its genital branch supplies cremaster

The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve enters the spermatic cord coverings through the deep ring region and supplies cremaster.
Efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex.
Its femoral branch supplies skin below the middle of the inguinal ligament

The femoral branch enters the femoral sheath in front of the femoral artery and supplies the skin below the middle of the inguinal ligament.
Afferent limb of the cremasteric reflex in part.
It is crossed by the ureter and gonadal vessels

On psoas, the genitofemoral nerve is crossed by the ureter and gonadal vessels, and on the left also by the left colic vessels and inferior mesenteric vein.
It lies behind the peritoneum.
It is motor to sartorius

The femoral branch has no motor fibres; sartorius is supplied by the femoral nerve.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
Arises from the posterior divisions of L2 and L3 or from the femoral nerve

Last's gives two possible origins of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve: the posterior divisions of L2 and L3, or the femoral nerve.
It crosses iliacus.
Enters the thigh about 1 cm medial to the anterior superior iliac spine

It enters the thigh about 1 cm medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, in a tunnel behind or through the inguinal ligament.
A site of entrapment.
May be compressed to cause meralgia paraesthetica

Compression here (or traction by transversus fibres from the iliac fascia) causes meralgia paraesthetica: burning pain on the lateral thigh.
Common in obesity or tight belts.
Supplies the skin of the medial thigh

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve supplies the anterolateral and lateral thigh, not the medial thigh.
The medial thigh is supplied by the obturator and femoral (medial cutaneous) nerves.
It enters the thigh lateral to the femoral sheath

The femoral nerve enters the thigh lateral to the femoral sheath, lying in the gutter between psoas and iliacus, outside the sheath.
"NAVY" from lateral to medial: nerve, artery, vein, Y-fronts.
It supplies iliacus within the abdomen

The femoral nerve supplies iliacus within the abdomen by two or three branches.
Psoas gets direct branches from the roots.
Its nerve to vastus medialis travels in the adductor canal and supplies the knee

The nerve to vastus medialis travels in the adductor canal and gives a branch to the knee joint (Hilton's law).
It also supplies the capsule.
The saphenous nerve crosses the femoral artery from medial to lateral in the adductor canal

In the adductor canal the saphenous nerve crosses the femoral artery anteriorly from lateral to medial, not medial to lateral.
It then leaves between sartorius and gracilis.
Femoral artery

The femoral artery runs through the adductor canal and always lies between the saphenous nerve and the femoral vein.
It leaves through the adductor hiatus.
Saphenous nerve

The saphenous nerve runs in the canal and leaves it between sartorius and gracilis.
It does not pass through the hiatus.
Nerve to vastus medialis in its upper part

The nerve to vastus medialis runs with the femoral vessels in the upper part of the adductor canal before entering the muscle.
It also supplies the knee.
Femoral vein

Last's says the femoral vein spirals from medial to the artery in the femoral triangle to lateral at the adductor hiatus.
All four true: E.
It emerges from the medial border of psoas

The obturator nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas and crosses the pelvic brim medial to the sacroiliac joint.
It runs along the side wall to the obturator canal.
Its anterior division supplies adductor longus, brevis and gracilis

Its anterior division supplies adductor longus, adductor brevis and gracilis (and sometimes pectineus), and also the hip joint.
It lies in front of adductor brevis.
Its posterior division supplies the knee joint

Its posterior division supplies the knee joint, explaining referred knee pain in hip disease.
A child with knee pain may have hip pathology.
Its posterior division supplies the ischial part of adductor magnus

The posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor (pubic) part of adductor magnus. The ischial (hamstring) part is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic nerve.
Adductor magnus has a dual supply.

questions.s: Branches of the sacral plexus from posterior divisions include the:
o: Superior gluteal nerve

The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) is from the posterior divisions of the sacral plexus.
It supplies gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae.
Nerve to quadratus femoris

Last's says the nerve to quadratus femoris (L4, L5, S1) is from the anterior divisions.
It also supplies inferior gemellus.
Tibial part of the sciatic nerve

The tibial part of the sciatic nerve (L4 to S3) comes from the anterior divisions. The common peroneal part is from the posterior divisions.
Tibial = flexor.
Pudendal nerve

The pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) arises from the anterior rami before they divide (Last's treats it separately).
Answer A: 1 only.

questions.s: Concerning nerves of the gluteal region:
o: The superior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis

The superior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis, runs between gluteus medius and minimus and ends in tensor fasciae latae.
Its injury gives a Trendelenburg gait.
The inferior gluteal nerve is L5, S1 and S2

The inferior gluteal nerve is L5, S1 and S2 and supplies gluteus maximus.
It leaves below piriformis.
The nerve to obturator internus hooks around the base of the ischial spine

The nerve to obturator internus hooks around the base of the ischial spine, lateral to the pudendal vessels, and also supplies superior gemellus.
It re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen.
The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve lies deep to the sciatic nerve

Last's says the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve is superficial to the sciatic nerve, and the nerve to quadratus femoris is deep to it.
So it does not lie deep.
It emerges below piriformis, lateral to the inferior gluteal and pudendal bundles

The sciatic nerve emerges below piriformis, lateral to the inferior gluteal and pudendal bundles, and lies on the ischium over the posterior part of the acetabulum.
So posterior hip dislocation can damage it.
Its blood supply includes a branch of the inferior gluteal artery, a remnant of the axial artery

The artery to the sciatic nerve, a branch of the inferior gluteal, is the remnant of the embryonic axial artery of the limb.
Occasionally it persists as a large vessel.
The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by its tibial part

The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common peroneal part. All other hamstrings and the ischial part of adductor magnus are supplied by the tibial part.
The short head came from the extensor compartment.
It may divide high, with the peroneal part piercing piriformis

The sciatic nerve may divide high, with the peroneal part piercing piriformis while the tibial part runs normally below it.
A cause of piriformis syndrome.
Divides behind the lateral femoral condyle

The common peroneal nerve divides in the substance of peroneus longus, around the neck of the fibula, not behind the lateral femoral condyle.
That is where it is vulnerable to fractures and plaster casts.
Gives rise to the sural nerve

The sural nerve arises from the tibial nerve. The common peroneal gives the peroneal communicating nerve, which joins it.
The sural is mainly tibial.
Supplies tibialis posterior

Tibialis posterior is supplied by the tibial nerve.
The common peroneal supplies the anterior and lateral compartments.
Gives the lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf

The common peroneal nerve gives the lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf, which pierces the roof of the popliteal fossa over the lateral head of gastrocnemius.
Answer D: 4 only.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus longus and brevis

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies peroneus longus and brevis, then perforates the deep fascia about halfway down the leg.
Then it supplies the skin of the dorsum.
The deep peroneal nerve supplies extensor digitorum brevis

The deep peroneal nerve supplies extensor digitorum brevis and the skin of the first web space (cleft).
A small patch of sensory loss.
The deep peroneal nerve lies medial to the anterior tibial artery throughout the leg

Last's says the deep peroneal nerve runs lateral to the anterior tibial vessels and lies lateral to dorsalis pedis on the foot (it may cross the artery in the leg).
So "medial throughout" is wrong.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot

The superficial peroneal nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot, except the first cleft (deep peroneal) and the lateral border (sural).
A useful sensory map.
It is the most superficial of the main structures in the popliteal fossa

The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the main structures in the popliteal fossa; the popliteal vein always lies between the artery and the nerve.
From superficial to deep: nerve, vein, artery.
It supplies all the muscles arising in the popliteal fossa

The tibial nerve supplies all the muscles arising in the popliteal fossa, including gastrocnemius, plantaris, soleus and popliteus.
All the calf muscles.
It divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves deep to the flexor retinaculum

The tibial nerve divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves deep to the flexor retinaculum, behind the medial malleolus.
In the tarsal tunnel.
The medial calcanean nerve supplies the skin of the lateral border of the foot

The medial calcanean nerve supplies the weight-bearing skin of the heel. The sural nerve supplies the lateral border of the foot.
Heel pain can come from its entrapment.
Adductor hallucis

Adductor hallucis is supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
Like adductor pollicis by the deep ulnar.
Flexor hallucis brevis

The medial plantar nerve supplies flexor digitorum brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical, like the median nerve in the hand.
A neat analogy.
Flexor digiti minimi brevis

Flexor digiti minimi brevis is supplied by the superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
The lateral plantar is the ulnar equivalent.
The first lumbrical

The medial plantar nerve supplies the first lumbrical; the lateral three are supplied by the deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve.
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Structures piercing the roof of the popliteal fossa include the:
o: Tibial nerve

The tibial nerve lies within the popliteal fossa, the most superficial of its main contents, but does not pierce the roof.
It runs down the middle of the fossa.
Popliteal artery

The popliteal artery is the deepest of the main contents, lying on the floor.
It is at risk in supracondylar fractures.
Common peroneal nerve

The common peroneal nerve runs along the lateral boundary, medial to biceps. Its branches (lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf and peroneal communicating nerve) pierce the roof, not the nerve itself.
A subtle distinction.
Small saphenous vein

Last's lists four structures piercing the roof: the small saphenous vein, the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, the peroneal communicating nerve and the lateral cutaneous nerve of the calf.
Answer D: 4 only.
Arises from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa

The sural nerve arises from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa and lies in the groove between the two heads of gastrocnemius.
It is often harvested for nerve grafts.
Pierces the deep fascia halfway down the leg

It pierces the deep fascia about halfway down the leg, where it is joined by the peroneal communicating nerve.
Then it runs down superficially.
Lies medial to the small saphenous vein behind the medial malleolus

The sural nerve runs lateral to the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus, not medial to it behind the medial malleolus.
The saphenous nerve accompanies the great saphenous vein medially.
Ends on the lateral side of the little toe

The sural nerve ends on the lateral side of the little toe, supplying the lateral border of the foot.
S1 territory.

questions.s: Regarding the segmental supply of lower limb movements:
o: Hip flexion and adduction are L2 and L3

Hip flexion and adduction are L2 and L3; hip extension and abduction are L4 and L5.
"Flex and adduct high."
Knee extension is L3 and L4

Knee extension is L3 and L4; knee flexion is L5 and S1.
Knee jerk L3/4.
Ankle plantarflexion is S1 and S2

Ankle plantarflexion is S1 and S2; dorsiflexion is L4 and L5.
Ankle jerk S1.
Inversion of the foot is S1

Inversion of the foot (tibialis anterior and posterior) is L4. Eversion is L5 and S1.
So S1 is wrong for inversion.

questions.s: Concerning nerve supply anomalies noted by Last:
o: Tibialis posterior is supplied by L4 although it is a plantarflexor

Last's notes that tibialis posterior is supplied by L4, although it is a plantarflexor, to match its inverting partner tibialis anterior.
Segmental supply follows action at a joint, here inversion.
Gluteus maximus and obturator internus are L5, S1 and S2

Gluteus maximus and obturator internus are L5, S1 and S2; the other buttock muscles are L4, L5 and S1.
A lower supply.
The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common peroneal part of the sciatic nerve

The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common peroneal part of the sciatic nerve, because it migrated from the extensor compartment.
The long head is tibial.
Pectineus may receive supply from both femoral and obturator nerves

Pectineus may receive supply from both the femoral and obturator nerves. Pectineus, adductor magnus and biceps femoris all have a dual supply.
All four true: E.

questions.s: Regarding dermatomes of the lower limb:
o: L1 supplies the inguinal region and anterior scrotum

L1 supplies the inguinal region, anterior scrotum and root of the penis via the ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves.
It lies just above the axial line.
L5 supplies the dorsum of the foot and great toe

L5 supplies the dorsum of the foot and great toe, and the lateral leg.
L5 radiculopathy numbs the big toe.
S1 supplies the lateral border of the foot and sole

S1 supplies the lateral border of the foot and the sole, and the lateral malleolus.
Little toe numbness suggests S1.
S3 supplies the posterior thigh

S2 supplies the posterior thigh and leg. S3 supplies the sitting area of the buttock and the posterior scrotum.
Saddle anaesthesia is S3 to S5.
The main blood supply to the femoral head in adults is from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery

In adults the main blood supply to the femoral head comes from the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery; the artery of the ligamentum teres is minor.
Displaced intracapsular fractures tear them, causing avascular necrosis.
The iliofemoral ligament resists extension

The iliofemoral ligament resists extension of the hip; it is the strongest ligament in the body.
It lets us stand with little muscular effort.
It is supplied by the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves

The hip joint is supplied by the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves (including the nerve to quadratus femoris).
Hip pain can refer to the knee.
The neck of the femur ossifies from a separate epiphysis

Last's says the neck of the femur is the upper end of the shaft and ossifies as part of it, not from a separate epiphysis.
The head and trochanters have their own epiphyses.

questions.s: The knee joint receives nerve supply from the:
o: Femoral nerve via the nerve to vastus medialis

The femoral nerve supplies the knee via the nerve to vastus medialis (Last's, Hilton's law).
Also via the other vasti branches.
Genicular branches of the tibial and common peroneal nerves

Genicular branches of the tibial and common peroneal nerves (from the sciatic) supply the knee joint.
Posterior and lateral aspects.
Posterior division of the obturator nerve

The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies the knee, running with the femoral artery through the adductor hiatus.
The basis of referred hip-to-knee pain.
Saphenous nerve via its infrapatellar branch

The saphenous nerve supplies the front of the knee via its infrapatellar branch, contributing to the patellar plexus.
All four true: E.

questions.s: Regarding ossification in the lower limb:
o: The centre for the lower end of the femur appears at birth and is medicolegal evidence of maturity

The centre for the lower end of the femur appears just before birth, so its presence is medicolegal evidence of a full-term fetus.
It is the first epiphysis to ossify.
The fibula is exceptional in that its upper (growing) end ossifies later than its lower end

The fibula is exceptional: its upper (growing) end ossifies later than its lower end (head at about 4 years, lower end at about 1 year).
Usually the growing end ossifies first.
The cuboid ossifies at about 9 months of fetal life

The cuboid ossifies at about 9 months of fetal life, and its presence is also evidence of maturity.
Like the lower femoral epiphysis.
Most growth in length of the lower limb occurs at the hip

Growth in length of the lower limb proceeds more rapidly at the knee than at the hip or ankle.
"From the knee I flee."

questions.s: Concerning veins of the lower limb:
o: The great saphenous vein marks the preaxial border of the limb

The great saphenous vein marks the preaxial border of the lower limb; the small saphenous marks the postaxial border.
A developmental landmark.
The great saphenous vein passes in front of the medial malleolus with the saphenous nerve

The great saphenous vein passes in front of the medial malleolus with the saphenous nerve, a site for venous cutdown.
The nerve can be caught in a ligature.
The femoral vein lies lateral to the femoral artery at the adductor hiatus

Last's says the femoral vein spirals from medial to the artery in the femoral triangle to lateral to it at the adductor hiatus.
It becomes the popliteal vein.
The small saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein

The small saphenous vein pierces the roof of the popliteal fossa to drain into the popliteal vein, not the femoral vein.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
